title: Anger online
hookLine: a hard word online still hurts a person
tomorrow: can giving someone your full attention be a way to love them?

cards: A comment under a highlight clip, from an account with no face and no real name: you're trash. The reply box is already open. Three sharp sentences arrive almost on their own, and they're good ones, honestly.
The thumb hovers. It stings, and it's late. What do you type back to a stranger who started it?
The answer starts with something the screen hides.

teach.b: First, what the Bible doesn't say. It doesn't say never be angry. Paul, in Ephesians, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Be angry, and sin not. Let not the sun go down upon your anger."
Anger is allowed in the room. It just isn't handed the keyboard, and it isn't kept overnight.

teach.h: SLOW TO SPEAK, SLOW TO ANGER.
teach.b: James gives the order of operations: "swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger." The anger isn't the trouble in those verses; the speed is. Online, that order flips.
Fast to type, fast to post, and hearing comes last, if at all.

Proverbs gives the result of each choice: "A mild answer breaketh wrath: but a harsh word stirreth up fury." A harsh reply to a harsh comment just lights a second fire: two strangers, each sure the other one started it.

And here's what the screen hides: an account with no face is still a person reading, maybe a kid, maybe someone in a hard week. It runs the other way too; the comment that stung was read by a real person.
That's why it stung. So what to type back? Maybe nothing.
Maybe one mild line. Maybe write the angry version, read it once, and delete it.

how: Catholics examine their words, online and off, in an examination of conscience, and confess sins of speech in the sacrament of Penance; the Church's media messages urge kindness and truth online.

o: harsh words typed at people you can't see
a website that blocks rude comments
feeling upset after losing a game

games.q: anger and the reply box — tap the pairs.
p: swift to hear, slow to speak

s: the Bible says a Christian should never feel angry
be angry, and sin not: Ephesians 4:26.
James puts hearing first, speaking after, and anger last
swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger.
a harsh reply to a harsh comment calms things down
a harsh word stirreth up fury; a mild answer breaketh wrath.

games.q: at 11pm your dad sees a neighbor's angry post about street parking and starts drafting a long reply. what does today say?
o: wait till morning, then answer mildly, if at all.
post now while it's fresh, or the moment is gone.
reply politely, but answer every insult point by point.
games.why: James: slow to speak, slow to anger. Proverbs: a mild answer breaketh wrath. the sun going down is a deadline for the anger, not for the reply.

practice: If there's an angry version sitting somewhere, a text, a comment, an email, open it and read it once, slowly. Then delete it, and notice how your shoulders feel afterward.
If there isn't one, rest your hands in your lap and let one breath go out slower than it came in. Notice whether the anger is still there after the breath; it's allowed to be.

wordCard.voice: Anger online. Heat typed at a screen that lands on a person: fast to post, slow to take back, and read by someone real.

orig.note: Greek: be angry. the first word of Ephesians 4:26, followed by and sin not.

carryVoice: The line to keep: a person reads it, on both ends of every comment. See you next week.
